title: The Hatchery
story: You and NOVA are helping at a wildlife hatchery when the gate locks for the night. Open four locks by helping NOVA understand how animals reproduce.
escaped: The gate opens. NOVA now sorts animals by how young are born and gives honest ranges, not exact guesses.

locks.title: Born or hatched?
locks.intro: NOVA must sort animals into viviparous (give birth to young ones) and oviparous (lay eggs). Choose its clues, then test it on a whale and a bat.
locks.hint: A whale lives in water and a bat can fly, but both are mammals.
locks.learn: If an AI uses where an animal lives or whether it flies, the whale and the bat fool it. The clue that defines the groups, how the young are born, sorts both.

locks.title: Fix NOVA's reproduction facts
locks.intro: NOVA has matched animals with how they reproduce. Tick the matches that are wrong.

rows.label: Internal fertilisation
rows.why: fish eggs are fertilised outside the body, in water

locks.hint: Which animals lay eggs in water, where the sperm meet them outside the body?
locks.learn: An AI can't know an example is wrong unless someone checks. Careful labelling is a big part of making AI useful.

locks.title: Check NOVA's pond survey
locks.intro: NOVA is counting animals in the hatchery pond. Is it right? Decide and pick the fact that settles it.
locks.claim: Tadpoles and frogs are two different kinds of animal.
evidence: A tadpole changes into an adult frog by metamorphosis.
locks.hint: What does a tadpole grow into?
locks.learn: An AI that judges only by appearance can split one animal into two. Knowing the life cycle, the evidence from biology, corrects it.

locks.title: How many frogs?
locks.intro: Each year the hatchery counted how many of 100 frog eggs grew into adult frogs.
locks.question: NOVA predicts: 'Next year exactly 5 of 100 eggs will become frogs.' What is the honest prediction?
options: Probably about 4 to 8, because it changed from year to year; nobody can say the exact number.
All 100, because frogs lay many eggs.
None, because most eggs don't survive.
locks.hint: Look at all three years, not just one.
locks.learn: Good predictions show uncertainty. The counts vary because many eggs and tadpoles are eaten or damaged, which is why frogs lay so many eggs. A range is more honest than one exact number.
